\chapter{Introduction}
Warehouse robots must localise accurately
while the layout of shelves and pallets changes around them.
Maps built once and frozen quickly become stale,
so lifelong SLAM systems maintain and update a map over months of operation.

The central difficulty is deciding which observations
should update the long-term map
and which should be treated as transient clutter.
A wrong decision in either direction
either corrupts the map or wastes useful information.

This report describes a conservative update policy
based on observation consensus across sessions,
and evaluates it on data collected in a working distribution centre.

\chapter{Methods}
The estimator is a pose graph with switchable constraints
that can be disabled when loop closures disagree with the long-term map.

The information gain of a candidate loop closure is \frac{1}{2}$ of the log determinant
ratio of the two covariance blocks involved,
and closures below a threshold are rejected outright.
Robust kernels down-weight the constraints that come from dynamic objects.

Sessions that disagree with the consensus map
are quarantined and re-examined after the next session arrives.
A quarantined session is merged only when its landmarks
are confirmed by at least two independent later sessions.
